stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: Iran War Victims Put Trump’s Power Grab On Trial
stories.text: Families of victims of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran just filed an unprecedented lawsuit asking a federal judge to decide a constitutional question Washington has evaded for decades: Can a president wage war without the approval of Congress? Attorneys behind the lawsuit, filed on behalf of the members of the National Iranian American Council, say this is the first time people impacted by an unauthorized military intervention, rather than lawmakers, are legally challenging presidential war powers. The Constitution’s Declare War Clause vests the power to declare war in Congress, not the president. The suit is being brought on behalf of Iranian-Americans whose relatives have been killed, injured, or otherwise harmed by U.S. strikes in Iran. “Nobody has tried this approach,” said Alan Morrison, a public interest lawyer representing the plaintiffs who has argued 20 cases before the Supreme Court — including one that has been interpreted to limit Congress’ ability to check presidential power. “We have a different group of plaintiffs, the people here who are suffering the war as the plaintiffs. stories.author: Ken Klippenstein
stories.title: Trump Announces New “AI Force”
stories.text: Space Force personnel Fundraising fell off a cliff this summer. Not accepting a dime in corporate ad money allows me to be genuinely independent; but it also means I’m ENTIRELY dependent on readers like you to survive. “I am forming the AI Force, much like I did [the] Space Force,” Donald Trump said last Saturday. Almost immediately, the AI shark tank started circling, eager to shape the president’s musings into something concrete, something that would benefit — them. It’s a Washington playbook and a kind of Rorschach test: the movers and shakers, the experts and the moguls telling you what the president “meant,” what an AI Force should be, whether it’s needed, and if it’s not, what’s needed instead. It’s a trillion-dollar Christmas wishlist you’re paying for but have no say in the contents, which will dictate the future of AI. Trump’s AI Force announcement A seventh military branch, alongside the Air Force, Army, Coast Guard, Marine Corps, Navy, and Space? Another military command alongside Cyber Command or Strategic Command? Another powerful agency like NSA? stories.author: Drop Site team
stories.title: Democratic Party Consultants Surround Troy Jackson with Pro-Israel Donors
stories.text: The Troy Jackson campaign in Maine may have found a new way to measure just how far Democratic Party consultants are able to drag a candidate away from his grassroots supporters. This week, as Jackson ventured into the Facebook group set up for his volunteers, he was facing a legion of Maine supporters expressing a deep sense of betrayal, following an exposé by Rebecca Traister in New York Magazine , which had laid out in precise detail how a squadron of mostly out-of-state political consultants had done as much as possible to drain the life from Jackson and his campaign. In the Facebook group, Jackson’s defense of his campaign, and his attack on the reporting, was considered so condescending that supporters concluded there was no way that Jackson himself was running the account—and promptly kicked Jackson out of his own Facebook group, with less than six weeks until election day. Jackson, it turned out, was indeed still manning his own Facebook account, and he has since been allowed back in. stories.author: Matt Taibbi
stories.title: Live Free Speech Discussion, 2:00 PM ET Today: Interview With Russian Journalist Dimitri Simes
stories.text: Racket readers should recall an interview published in this space in March with Dimitri Simes, a prominent Russian journalist who in August of 2024 became inveigled in one of the strangest and most disturbing speech cases of our times. While he and wife Anastasia Rurikova Simes were away, the FBI raided his Virginia home, seizing all his possessions but one. “My handgun,” Simes said. “They put it on my night table.” A month later, Simes was indicted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”), charged essentially with violating a sanctions regime by hosting a television program in Russian, in Russia. It was “a totally unprecedented use of the sanctions laws,” said Michel Paradis, one of several attorneys representing Simes. Paradis has worked on some of the more vexing national security cases of this era, including representation of Guantanamo Bay detainees. In the Simes case, Paradis — who’s written books about Dwight Eisenhower and the extraordinary flight over Tokyo by the “Doolittle Raiders ” — finds a prosecution with few historical analogs. stories.author: Judd Legum
stories.title: PopInfo Weekly: Stocks, smears, and settlements
stories.text: MAGA Inc., President Trump’s super PAC, has spent nearly $2.5 million on ads attacking Democrats for making stock trades while in Congress and in some instances failing to disclose the trades on time. What the ads don’t mention is that Trump himself has traded more securities since returning to office than all members of Congress combined (and often reported them late). Trump’s trades since 2025 could be worth up to $2.87 billion. Between September 5 and September 21, Elon Musk’s America PAC spent about $1 million on ads accusing Democratic candidates of supporting “taxpayer-funded sex change surgeries on kids.” The catch? None of these candidates have said they support taxpayer funding for such surgeries (which are extremely rare), and several explicitly oppose the proceedures. On Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) and 11 other state attorneys general settled a lawsuit to block Paramount, which is controlled by the Trump-supporting Ellison family, from acquiring Warner Bros. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: AI Regulation Was Coming. Then Trump Killed It.
stories.text: The investigation below raises a disturbing question: What if rogue AI agents are learning from the secrecy and rule-breaking of the humans who created them? Two years before this month’s nationwide panic over the apocalyptic potential of artificial intelligence, a first wave of Silicon Valley resignations began — and so did the omens of human extinction. As OpenAI’s safety officials resigned or were pushed out, they made headlines warning about the company’s lax safety standards and reckless deployment of powerful AI models. Soon after, Biden officials decided to act: On the 2024 anniversary of 9/11, they began advancing a first-of-its-kind rule to require AI companies to tell regulators exactly what kinds of experiments they were running at the edge of the technological frontier. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: The Machines Escaped. Their Masters Did So First.
stories.text: “Misalignment.” In the wake of artificial intelligence hacks, break-ins, and mini-disasters, that’s what technologists call the terrifying gap between what we want AI to do and what AI is actually doing. But much of what we are seeing is better described as AI’s accelerated super-alignment with the mundane behaviors of its Silicon Valley creators. Take the infamous hack of Hugging Face , in which OpenAI’s agents broke out of their sandbox and hacked another company, unbeknownst to their programmers. In that debacle, the most frightening behavior was the autonomous agents reportedly collaborating with each other to evade rules and hide crucial information from their human overseers. News of the incident read like a scary Skynet storyline from The Terminator franchise. But what’s just as creepy is how the AI agents’ efforts to limit transparency also mimicked the kind of devious human conduct that’s increasingly common here in the offline world. That includes the conduct of OpenAI’s team – both during the investigation of the Hugging Face breach and in its previous lobbying in Washington, as The Lever today reports .
